content: In semi-arid and arid ecosystems, vegetation density (NDVI) correlates strongly with cumulative rainfall, but the relationship is non-linear and mediated by soil water-holding capacity: degraded low-SOC soils convert a smaller fraction of rainfall into plant-available soil moisture due to increased runoff, meaning vegetation response to a given rainfall amount is systematically lower on degraded land than on healthy soil.
source: IPCC AR6 Working Group II, Chapter 4: Water (2022)
quantitative_impact: Degraded soils convert up to 30% less rainfall into usable soil moisture

content: IPCC AR6 WG2 identifies that many staple crops (wheat, maize) experience significant yield penalties when daytime temperatures exceed 30-34°C during flowering and grain-fill stages, with yield loss estimated at 5-10% per degree Celsius above the optimal threshold. Semi-arid regions are projected to see increasing frequency of these heat-stress events under continued warming.
source: IPCC AR6 Working Group II, Chapter 5: Food, Fibre and Other Ecosystem Products (2022)
quantitative_impact: 5-10% yield loss per °C above optimal threshold during flowering/grain-fill

content: IPCC AR6 highlights diversified cropping systems (intercropping, agroforestry, drought-tolerant varieties) as a key climate adaptation strategy, showing 15-30% smaller yield variance under drought years compared to monocultures, because different species/varieties have staggered water demand peaks and root architectures that access different soil depths.
source: IPCC AR6 Working Group II, Chapter 5 (2022); FAO Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook
quantitative_impact: 15-30% lower yield variance under drought with diversified systems

content: Vegetative cover, particularly tree canopy, reduces soil surface evaporation and moderates the local water balance by increasing infiltration and reducing peak soil temperatures. Removal of tree cover in semi-arid basins has been linked to measurable declines in local rainfall recycling, since transpired moisture from vegetation contributes to downwind precipitation formation.
source: Ellison, D. et al. (2017) Global Environmental Change: Trees, forests and water
quantitative_impact: Deforestation reduces regional moisture recycling contribution to rainfall by 10-30% in some basins

content: Semi-arid regions are defined by an aridity index (precipitation/potential evapotranspiration) of 0.2-0.5, typically receiving 250-600mm annual rainfall concentrated in short, high-intensity events with high inter-annual variability. This variability, rather than total rainfall alone, is a primary driver of vegetation stress and necessitates water-harvesting and soil-moisture-conserving practices.
source: UNCCD & FAO, Aridity Zones Classification (UNEP 1992, updated FAO 2019)
quantitative_impact: Semi-arid zones: 250-600mm annual rainfall, aridity index 0.2-0.5

content: IPCC AR6 WG3 estimates that improved cropland and grassland management (agroforestry, cover cropping, reduced tillage, rotational grazing) collectively hold a global technical mitigation potential of 2-4 GtCO2-eq/year by 2030, representing one of the largest and most cost-effective land-based climate mitigation levers alongside afforestation.
source: IPCC AR6 Working Group III, Chapter 7 (2022)
quantitative_impact: 2-4 GtCO2-eq/year global mitigation potential from improved land management

content: Tree cover and shelterbelts provide microclimate buffering, reducing understorey wind speed and peak temperatures, which lowers crop water stress and evapotranspiration demand. Field trials in semi-arid agroforestry systems report 12-18% improved effective water-use efficiency for intercropped species relative to open-field monoculture.
source: FAO 2021 Conservation Agriculture Report; ICRAF Agroforestry Microclimate Studies
quantitative_impact: +12-18% water-use efficiency under agroforestry microclimate buffering

content: Köppen-Geiger and aridity-index-based climate classification places regions broadly into tropical (high, consistent rainfall/temperature), arid (aridity index <0.2), semi-arid (0.2-0.5), temperate (moderate, seasonal), and humid/continental zones. Latitude bands roughly correlate: equatorial ±10° = tropical; 15-35° often arid/semi-arid (subject to local topography and ocean currents); 35-55° = temperate; >55° = boreal/polar.
source: Köppen-Geiger Climate Classification (Kottek et al. 2006 update)

content: Pollinator foraging activity, particularly for wild bees, declines sharply above ambient temperatures of 35-38°C, as thermal stress limits flight muscle performance and increases desiccation risk. In warming semi-arid regions, this creates a growing mismatch between crop flowering periods and effective pollinator activity windows.
source: IPCC AR6 Working Group II, Chapter 2: Terrestrial and Freshwater Ecosystems (2022)
quantitative_impact: Pollinator foraging activity drops sharply above 35-38°C ambient temperature

content: Low-cost water-harvesting structures (contour bunds, half-moon pits/zai pits, check dams) used widely in Sahelian and South Asian semi-arid agriculture can raise effective plant-available soil moisture by 20-40%, restoring degraded land productivity even without increasing total rainfall, by capturing and concentrating runoff into the root zone.
source: FAO 2021, Water Harvesting Techniques for Dryland Agriculture
quantitative_impact: +20-40% plant-available soil moisture from water-harvesting structures
